head: Gemini models explained: Flash-Lite, Hydrogen, Pro, Argon and Carbon
dek: The Gemini app now lists five models, and which ones you can pick depends on your plan: without a Google AI plan you get Auto or Flash-Lite, AI Plus adds Hydrogen, AI Pro adds Pro and Argon, and only AI Ultra gets Carbon.

p: Google's Gemini help page lists five models in the app's picker. Flash-Lite is for quick answers and light tasks. Hydrogen balances speed and ability in chats and tasks. Pro is for complex prompts, coding and problems that need more thought.

Argon is meant for complex, multi-step work, and Carbon for long, difficult problems. Google says Carbon uses more tokens than Argon to explore a problem and check its own work, so it points most everyday knowledge work to Argon and the harder, open-ended jobs to Carbon.

sections.h: Three new models in five weeks
p: Gemini 4 Argon was announced on October 13 for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app and in AI Mode in Search. Gemini 4 Carbon followed on November 10: it had gone to cybersecurity defenders two weeks earlier, and it is rolling out to AI Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app, AI Mode and Google Antigravity.

Gemini 4 Hydrogen came out on November 12. It reaches far more people than the other two: Google says it now powers answers in Google Search for all users worldwide, and free users of the Gemini app get it through automatic model selection.

An account without a Google AI plan can choose Auto or Flash-Lite. With Auto on, Gemini picks the model and thinking level for each prompt: most prompts go to Flash-Lite, and ones that need more reasoning may go to Hydrogen. With Auto off, every answer comes from Flash-Lite.

So on the free tier you can't pick Hydrogen yourself, and you can't tell in advance which model will answer. You can check afterwards: tap More on an answer, then See response details, and it names the model used.

Google AI Plus costs $4.99 a month in the US and lets you chat with Flash-Lite or Hydrogen. Google AI Pro, at $19.99 a month, adds Pro and Argon, and its Task Mode can use Hydrogen and Argon. Google AI Ultra starts at $99.99 a month, with a $199.99 tier for 20 times the usage; it has Flash-Lite, Hydrogen, Argon and Carbon for chats, and Hydrogen, Argon and Carbon for tasks.

Google gives no exact message limits on the help page. It says larger models and higher thinking levels use up more of your allowance, and that a paid plan's chat carries on with Flash-Lite once you reach the limit. Work and school accounts depend on their Workspace license, and Google notes that availability can change.

sections.h: How to switch models and thinking levels
p: With a plan, tap the model name at the bottom of the chat box and pick another; a lock icon means the model needs a higher plan. You can also pick a thinking level of Low, Medium or High. If you don't, it stays on Low. Your choice sticks to that conversation, also when you come back to it later.
To turn automatic selection on or off, open the menu, then Settings and Usage limits; the switch is at the bottom of that page.

sections.h: For developers and apps built on Gemini
p: Apps that use Gemini through Google's API pay per million tokens. Hydrogen costs $1.50 for input and $7.50 for output. Argon and Carbon cost $2 and $10 at their introductory price, which rises to $4 and $20 on November 30, 2026.

means: If you use Gemini for free, Auto decides whether you get Flash-Lite or Hydrogen for each prompt, and Google Search answers now run on Hydrogen. Picking a model yourself starts with the $4.99 AI Plus plan.
todo: To see which model answered, tap More on a response and choose See response details. On a paid plan, pick the model and thinking level at the bottom of the chat box, and remember that High thinking and larger models use up your allowance faster.
